extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in religion, philosophy, and literary argument
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles from G.K. Chesterton's essay discussing what keeps minds 'sane' — criteria about beliefs, reason, mysticism, humility, will, and the proper relation of virtues. Useful for assessing philosophical positions or crafting arguments that preserve human health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the reductive completeness of materialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism, as an explanation, has an 'insane simplicity' — it may 'cover everything' yet 'leave everything out' and produce a cosmos 'smaller than our world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: systems that explain all phenomena purely mechanistically and thereby ignore 'the real things of the earth' (fighting peoples, proud mothers, first love, fear on the sea). If a philosophical scheme makes the parts seem greater than the whole, treat it as unduly narrowing human experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge beliefs by relation to psychological health (not only truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton distinguishes the relation of creeds to health from their relation to objective verity; some doctrines may be true but unhealthy, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an idea, ask whether it preserves hope, courage, poetry, initiative and other human qualities, not only whether it is logically or empirically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit manifold and miscellaneous complexity in the universe
rubrics_metrics.description: A sane worldview admits that the universe is manifold and even miscellaneous — the Christian can accept settled order and miracle; the sane man knows he is complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion favors systems that allow multiple, even contradictory, aspects of reality (beast, devil, saint, citizen, madman) rather than single‑toned explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid total vetoes that banish all possibility of the spiritual
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism is criticized for not being 'allowed to retain even the tiniest imp' — its pure veto excludes any speck of spiritualism or miracle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject belief-systems that insist on absolute negative claims that preclude any alternative phenomena; allow room for unexpected or 'miraculous' instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical livability over theoretical completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Both madmen and pure materialists can offer unanswerable theories that are 'intolerable' in life; theoretical completeness that cripples humanity indicates madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess philosophies by their consequences in practice: if a theory makes everyday action, relationships, or moral agency impossible, it's disqualified regardless of internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve human qualities (hope, courage, poetry, initiative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialist deductions that gradually destroy 'his humanity' (hope, courage, poetry, initiative) are judged unhealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A healthy creed should sustain and encourage these human qualities; if a doctrine induces fatalism or emotional numbness, it's failing the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not negate moral agency or responsibility (reject destructive determinism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinism 'binds, not to loose' — it takes away freedom to raise, curse, thank, justify, punish, resist temptations, incite mobs, make resolutions, or pardon sinners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophies should allow for moral speech-acts and practices (praise, punishment, exhortation). Anti-pattern: doctrines that render appeals to will and moral exhortation meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain the possibility of persuasion and moral improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If sins are inevitable, persuasion is prevented; determinism 'stops the kind exhortation' and is 'quite as likely to lead to cruelty as... to cowardice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer systems that permit appeals to conscience and nurture reformative measures rather than only environmental or purely coercive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirm the reality and existence of others (avoid solipsistic egoism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solipsistic skeptic who believes everything began in himself destroys relations: friends become mythologies he created, and the world collapses into his private nightmare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject philosophies that reduce other minds and external reality to mere projections of the self. Value doctrines that sustain interpersonal reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject extremes that are 'complete in theory and crippling in practice'
rubrics_metrics.description: Both extremes (absolute materialism and absolute solipsism) exhibit completeness in theory but cripple practical life and humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor balanced doctrines that may be less 'complete' formally but enable flourishing action and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a central mystery to preserve psychological health (mysticism keeps men sane)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As long as you have mystery you have health; when you destroy mystery you create morbidity.' Ordinary men are mystics who 'permit the twilight' and keep one foot in fairyland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow an irreducible mystery or unexplained core in your worldview; anti-pattern: attempts to render everything lucid leading to soullessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value truth over consistency when necessary (tolerate contradictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sane man 'has permitted the twilight' and 'has always cared more for truth than for consistency' — he accepts contradictory truths together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two apparent truths conflict, accept both and live with the paradox (stereoscopic spiritual sight) rather than forcing a unitary consistent theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mystery as a springboard for clarity elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The mystic allows one thing to be mysterious, and everything else becomes lucid.' Putting dogma in central darkness enables clarity in daily relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural guidance: reserve an inexplicable core (dogma/mystery); test whether this enables clear, humane behavior (e.g., courteous relations, moral actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a paradoxical, growth‑permitting symbol (cross) over closed perfection (circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross, with a paradox at its center, 'can extend its four arms for ever without altering its shape,' whereas a closed circle is fixed and bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek closed perfect systems; favor frameworks that incorporate central contradictions enabling expansion and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure intellectualism has 'heat' and purpose, not just abstract light
rubrics_metrics.description: Detached intellectualism is 'moonshine' — light without heat and secondary light from a dead world; Apollo combined imagination and sanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual endeavors should connect with human needs and passions; avoid sterile abstractions divorced from life and healing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground reason in proper first principles (avoid 'reason used without root')
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief mark of insanity: 'reason used without root' — thinking without proper first principles leads to madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before complex deduction, ensure foundational commitments (belief in reality, moral intuitions, some form of authority) are in place; anti-pattern: endless skepticism that undercuts these foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that reason itself rests on a kind of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reason is itself a matter of faith' — it is an act of faith to assert that thoughts relate to reality; destroying divine authority can undermine human authority to think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of critiques that deny all authority; when assessing skepticism, account for the meta‑problem that reason presupposes trust in cognitive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve distinctness of things against over‑diffusive evolutionism or anti‑category views
rubrics_metrics.description: If evolution or similar doctrines deny the distinctness of 'things' (no ape, no man), thinking is undermined: 'You cannot think if there are no things to think about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain categories and objects as stable enough to permit thought and language; anti-pattern: radical nominalism or flux that erases object‑certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extreme pragmatism that rejects objective truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism is valid as a guide, but extreme pragmatism that tells a man to 'think what he must think and never mind the Absolute' removes the necessity to believe in objective truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking pragmatic criteria, retain commitment to some Absolute or objective truth required for coherent thought; balance human needs with honesty about fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specificity when praising volition (will must be particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worship of will in general is 'the negation of will'; to admire will generally is to refuse to choose — will's essence is that it is particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical test: praise particular acts or ends of will, not the abstract notion of willing itself. Anti-pattern: valorizing 'will' as a vague force without standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place humility in the right organ: doubt self, not truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Old humility restrained appetite and made men small to make their world large; new humility doubts 'the Divine Reason' and makes men doubtful about their aims, stalling action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage humility that motivates striving (doubt self so you work harder) rather than humility that paralyzes aims (doubt truth so you stop working).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate virtues; avoid isolated virtues run mad
rubrics_metrics.description: When virtues are 'let loose' from a coherent religious framework, they wander and do damage — pity without truth is often 'untruthful' and mercy without sin creates anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical dispositions in relation to others: truth must temper pity, and pity must temper truth. Anti-pattern: single-minded pursuit of one virtue to the exclusion of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against meta-skepticism that halts thought ('a thought that stops thought')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a thought that stops thought' — the complete skeptic ends by denying the right to think at all, asking why anything should go right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject philosophical moves that undermine the very possibility of reasoning or observation. Practical test: if a position eliminates the basis for any argument (including its own), it is self‑defeating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat doctrines partly by their life‑enabling consequences (reason as a defense of reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious authorities (creeds, hierarchies) were organized 'for the difficult defence of reason' — institutions sometimes preserved the conditions for thinking itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutions or doctrines, consider whether they historically or practically preserved conditions that permit sustained reasoning (education, language, authority structures).
